the result that crossing the protocol/application boundary typ-
ically suffers multiple data traversals. Additionally, the model
of application and network has been mainly a passive one: ap-                                       TCP
plications pre-bind buffers to store messages into; if the buffer
to store the message into depends on the message contents, or
the application has not installed enough bound buffers, the data                                     IP
is copied multiple times, obviously hurting performance.
    We have developed a system that provides efficient protocol
composition across both protocol and application boundaries                                       link level
and, due to its event model, allows applications to actively
participate in message processing (both in determining where
to place the message and in supplying operations to perform
on it). The system has a simple but powerful interface that has                 Figure 1: Protocol composition stack.

that dynamically compiles multiple data processing steps into
a single specialized memory loop.                                   protocol stack itself and are propagated downward until either

    
/ This is the main body of the receive ash for UDP. /                     
    
/ nbytes is the size of the message. /              
    
/ Note that the required checksum over the IP pseudoheader has /                       
    
/ been omitted for clarity.
                                    
int udp receive ash(void ash data, int nbytes) {
   struct udp udp hdr;
   int sum, left;

            
        / Initialize the checksum accumulation register which will be used in pipe. /                   
        p export(CKSUM PIPE, pipe cksum, 0);

                                            
        if(nbytes<sizeof(struct udp)) / Udp got too few bytes, abort now. /                
            return(ASH ABORT);

            
        / Slurp the UDP header into a local variable (udp hdr) /                  
            
        / In the process, run the checksum pipe on the header. /                   
            
        / If it fails, return abort. /  
        if(consume(&udp hdr, sizeof(struct udp), CKSUM PIPE) < 0)
                 
            / Should not happen since we have enough bytes /                  
            return(ASH ABORT);

        left = nbytes − sizeof(struct udp);

            
        / If there is a checksum in the UDP header, /                 
            
        / must finish the checksum computation at this point. /               
            
        / If the header checksum value is 0, no checksum was sent by the remote side. /                         
        if(udp hdr.cksum != 0) {

                 
                / Deliver rest of message to higher level layer, using the checksum pipe. /                 
                if (deliver(left, CKSUM PIPE) < 0) return(ASH ABORT);

                 
                / Read the checksum accumulation register to find out the final result /            
                 
                / of the checksum now that the deliver has finished. /             
                sum = p import(CKSUM PIPE, pipe cksum);

                 
                / Fold 32−bit sum to 16 bits and invert (part of the checksum computation). /                   
                sum = (unsigned short)˜inet fold(sum);

                         
                if(sum) / Should have summed to zero. Checksum failed. Abort.                  /
                    return(ASH ABORT);
        }
                     
        else { / No checksum to check /         
                 
                / Deliver rest of message with no pipe. /         
                if (deliver(left, ASH SPECIAL PIPE)<0) return(ASH ABORT);
        }

            
        / Ash succeeded! /      
        return(ASH SUCCESS);
}

    
/ This is the UDP receive commit handler. /                   
                                               
int udp rcommit(void ash data) { / Pass on success /                      
   return(ASH SUCCESS);
}

    
/ This is the UDP receive abort handler. /                
                                               
void udp rabort(void ash data) { / No cleanup to do; pass on failure. /                        
   return(ASH ABORT);
}

   Operation                                                                Description
   int consume(void *dst, int nbytes, int pipe id)                          Consume nbytes of message by copying it to dst while applying pipe
                                                                            pipe id. Used to consume headers, fragments, and application data.
                                                                            Derivatives of this function are provided to copy or skip over data.
   int deliver([ void *pre hdr, unsigned pre bytes, pipe id pre id, ]       Deliver nbytes of the incoming byte stream to the next protocol (on
               unsigned nbytes, pipe id pipe id                             send, this is the protocol immediately below the current protocol;
               [, void *post hdr, unsigned post bytes, pipe id post id ])   on receive it is the protocol above). The pipe pipe id will be applied
                                                                            when the data is touched. Optional arguments append data to the front
                                                                            (pre hdr) or back (post hdr) of the message; each of these pieces
                                                                            of data can be manipulated by their own pipes. deliver causes the
                                                                            protocol’s final code to be pushed. (deliver also has a more complex
                                                                            form that takes a list of data elements to append to the message.)
   int initiate(void *data, int nbytes)                                     Initiate a message send of nbytes of data. Causes the current proto-
                                                                            col’s send path to be invoked.

processing, its interface is both simple and powerful. A re-               August 1996.
stricted number of primitives can be used in regular ways to
perform a rich set of actions.
    An important practical benefit of our approach is that it
does not require source code in order to integrate layers. As a
result, it can be used to couple routines available only in system
libraries or even to routines that are dynamically linked in. The
most important benefit of this methodology is that the applica-
tion can be integrated into message processing in the same way
as protocols themselves. Such integration is crucial in order to
eliminate multiple data manipulations that would otherwise
result from crossing the application/protocol boundary.
